questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere with a very different culture and daily life than in Denmark which is why I was interested in going to Asia. Besides, I knew that Korea is a very safe country and it has such an interesting history and unique culture so I thought it would be a safe, interesting and fun place to go.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was do-able but not easy. SNU's website often changes automatically to Korean so it was a constant hassle to get information in English. Their systems for applying for classes is very different and the exchange students could have used more guidance on that in advance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We recieved a very long pdf file with info about everything at SNU.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy. I found housing within a few days after starting my search. I would definitely recommend living off-campus and not too far from the Gwanak area (where SNU is located). Seoul is huge so living in an area somewhat close to uni makes a huge difference, not only in terms of going to classes, but also in terms of social activities which are often in the area where most SNU students live. I also recommend having roommates, that was really nice for me, especially in the beginning when you know no one yet.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is more expensive than living on campus but more authentic and fun as well. In the dorms on campus, there are strict rules and you will most likely be sharing a small room with another student. Off campus, you are free to live your own life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was so complicated. First, there was a test-round where you could practice registering for courses. However, SNU forgot to tell the exchange students that the date for the test round had changed (they told os a few hours before it was supposed to start, meaning it was in the middle of the night) so we all missed it. Afterwards, there was a pre-registratiuon round where you coiuld put courses in your "shopping basket" and if the class then was not too popular, you would be registered automatically. Then after that, there was the real registration round where you could register for courses in yhour basket which was stressfull and on a first-come-first-serve basis. After that, there was a new round where you could apply for courses that were not yet full after the pre-registration round. So many exchange students had issues with getting even just one class that they wanted because the system was so different and stressfull. A while that, there were other registration rounds where you could apply for classes that were already full. By that time, I was already in Korea as it was only a week or so before classes started.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: None. Everyone got an e-mail from the international department at SNU explaining the proces very briefly, but from then on, it was your own problem.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Somewhat succesfull. It worked out in the end, but it took a lot of waking up in the middle of the night to see if some classes had gotten extra spots available and so.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You have to be very fast. If you log on one minute after the registration starts, classes will be full. Besides, have a list of alternative classes ready because you are most likely not to get all the classes you want (if any in the first place).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was much more variation in the course catalogue than at UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level was lower but the work load was heavier. I had presentations almost every week and often had small assignments to hand in and so. So there was more to do but the things you had to do were easier than at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: You are much more in contact with your professors than at UCPH. Classes are smaller and people are more involved and actively participating. In my classes, students took turns of presenting every week, so the students play a much bigger role than at UCPH. You could just lean back and do nothing in class, let alone not show up for classes regularly.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 1) Economic Development and Leadership in Asia, 2) Geopolitics and Political Economy of Space, 3) Public Policy and Community Wellbeing

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really liked the geopolitics course. The professor was very motivating and there was a really good atmosphere and learning environment in that class. The course about economic development in Asia was very easy and we never had mandatory readings, however we got to go on a really good study trip with all expenses paid, so that was really nice.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The ARC (alien registration card), mandatory health insurance

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries, especially fruit and vegetables, were very expensive. It was more expensive to cook a meal than to buy take out or go to a restaurant. Hence I rarely cooked. On the other hand, going out and eating out was very cheap. So was public transport and housing when traveling/going on weekend trips.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: SNU had lots of clubs, however most of them were in Korean. For the exchange students, there was "SNU Buddy" which was really good. They arranged activities every week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: SNU Buddy. It was great for meeting lots of other exchange students as well as the Korean buddies. Every exchange student also got a personal Korean buddy from SNU buddy who could help you if you had any problems.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to as many different parts of Korea as you can. I especially enjoyed visiting the east coast (Gangneung for example) and the south west (e.g. the tea plantations in Boseong were really cool). Besides, nature in Korea is amazing so go climb a mountain, visit a bamboo forest, and go see the tea fields in the south. There are so many things to do in Korea, it is great.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was a bigger culture shock than I had expected. In the beginning, it was a challenge that almost no one spoke or understood English, but you get used to it pretty fast. There are cultural differences that you do not understand (e.g. that women have to cover their shoulders even when it's really hot in the summer), but you get used to it. It also suprised me how it feels standing out. As a Westerner, many people look at you and you sometimes feel like you do not fit in. But again, you get used to it. And you learn so much from being in a culture that is SO different from Copenhagen.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Again, join SNU Buddy. The Koreans who join that program are really interested in getting to know foreigners, so that is the easiest way to meet Koreans. Besides, just talk to people in your classes. The Koreans are often quite reserved but once you talk to them, they open up and are really nice people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The language barrier.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The going-out culture was really nice. People love going out for a meal and a drink (many drinks) together as often as possible.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Don't worry too much about the money, just enjoy being there while you can, 2) Join SNU Buddy and go to as many social activities as possible, 3) Live in an area not too far from campus

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Download Naver Maps (it is like Google Maps but for Korea) and Papago (an app that will safe you as it translates everything for you, even menu cards, the words on your washing machine etc)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many cool people. You meet people from all over the world with so many different experiences in life, and it completely changes your view on so many issues in the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Missing people at home. Some days, you just really wish you were at that party that all your friends at home are at, or that you could give your boyfriend a hug.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Going on exchange to Seoul has been an amaxing experience for me and I highly recommend it. Don't worry too much about things, just go and it will all work out.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
